strength: A single dated plan inside ₹1.2 crore. It rushes the top 5 shades, re-cartons on Monday, refuses to order slow lines and gives an honest restock message in our voice that Tanvi would accept.
mistake: It counts the 3,900 held top-5 units as already inside the 9,100, so re-cartoning adds nothing to stock and a gap is assumed. The cap of 4 per shade cuts across artists like Farah, and the ₹699 palette cut is steep.
to10: Settle whether the held stock adds to the 9,100, which may close the 1–8 December gap. Exempt pros from the cap. Explain how the 4 foundation shades are chosen when there is no shade-level data.

strength: The maths is tight and shown: 76% of spend on hero shades, rush sizing that includes sale week at 2.5x, reorder points per line, and a Monday check sheet with triggers the ops lead can run.
mistake: It makes the same held-stock assumption, so it also plans a gap. Labelling the pro pre-book a 'bolder move' makes it read as an option when I asked for one plan. The back-order message is clunky ('That's a real date').
to10: Fold the pro pre-book into the main plan. Tighten the customer copy into our playful voice. Recheck whether re-cartoning lifts top-5 stock to cover until the rush order lands.

strength: A clean profit table against the 2.5 break-even. The budget split adds to exactly $240,000, its daily figures are worked out, and the base and cautious profit cases check out arithmetically.
mistake: It names broad 'women's flats' and 'sustainable shoes' as money-losers but never removes them. PMax keeps $128,000 with no negatives on those terms, so the projected 2.6 ROAS depends on hope.
to10: Add explicit negatives or caps on the broad and sustainable terms inside PMax. Add week 2–4 cut and grow rules beyond the reserve release, and add a recheck so the price mismatch does not come back after the next site price change.

strength: It names the $146,300 of loss-making spend and actually cuts it, with negatives and a products-only PMax. It gives clear month rules and a week-one table with an owner and a 'done when' for each step, and its 'test whether the cut spend builds brand' idea is a geo test with a stated cost.
mistake: Some claims are overstated or unclear: 'Google makes money only on brand' contradicts its own winners, and the $59,948 figure is unexplained. Adding brand negatives to bags Shopping is questionable, and it uses the British spelling 'colour'.
to10: Drop the overclaim in the opening line and explain the $2,000-a-day test cost. Reconsider the brand negatives in bags Shopping, and add a guard against the price mismatch recurring after the next site price change.

strength: Decisive opening that names the three fixes in order. It is honest about fit finder selection bias (it credits only half the 19-point gap) and adds a Christmas warning with a holdout. All of that is real owner thinking.
mistake: There is no real post-delivery fit help for first-time bra buyers; the delivered email just points back to the quiz. The savings are spread across monthly and 90-day figures with no single total, which makes them hard to rank by money.
to10: Add a bra fit-check message after delivery with practical try-on tips. Show one total saving per 90 days with the three fixes ranked by pounds. Make the swap sales figure easier to read.

strength: It opens with where the cost sits: £139,800 in returns, £31,360 in tickets, 6,076 tickets on days 3 to 5. It covers more of the journey, including a pre-dispatch fit check, practical bra try-on tips on delivery and a day-5 'How's the fit?' email. All are on-voice with one button each, and the savings table has a clear total.
mistake: It does not say outright that quiz users may differ from other buyers. The low-case 23.5% only hints at this. The 2-hour size switch rests on an operations assumption that may not hold, and the work order does not explain the Christmas timing risk.
to10: State the selection-bias caveat outright, flag the peak-season effect on the hold-out, and rank the three fixes by pounds saved in the summary.

strength: Honest money with checkable working. It shows a range, applies 6% monthly churn after 90 days, and gives a blunt warning: the pause does 80% of the work, and without it the flow keeps fewer people than today. That sets a clear critical path for the sprint.
mistake: The trip-over panel only lets people go. It gives no 'remind me before your next trip' or pause option for Greg-type learners. Also, the cancel button is inactive until a reason is picked, which comes close to the easy-cancel rule.
to10: Add an optional 'email me before my next trip' line for goal or trip-over learners. Keep the cancel button live at all times. Add a holdout group to prove the new rates. Trim a little to sit comfortably under 1,000 words.

strength: It covers more cases. There is a 'remind me in 3 or 6 months' option for trip-over, a smaller-goal option for learners who already set reminders, a cancel button that is always live, and a 10% holdout to test the assumptions. The build notes are concrete.
mistake: It keeps the 50% off for app-switchers, the same offer that 61% abandon. It also values those 67 people at full price while labelling it 'after discount'. The yearly figure of £136k assumes no churn and gives no range.
to10: Drop or justify the 50% off for switchers. Value discounted keeps at the discounted price. Apply realistic churn to the 12-month figure and give a low-to-high range. Flag that the whole gain depends on rebuilding the pause.

strength: It opens with a clear decision, then ranks the work by tickets we can remove and gives an honest range forecast (2,703 to 4,276) with correct working. The bolder idea of a balances-screen banner is costed and has its risk stated.
mistake: It writes a new Simplify debts article instead of rewriting the 38%-helpful 'How balances work' page, so that weak page stays live. It also never adds the 'undo delete' and 'restore' searches as search synonyms.
to10: Rewrite 'How balances work' itself to lead with Simplify debts, add search synonyms for the no-click terms, and include web (splitwise.com) steps and cancel-subscription steps in the articles.

strength: The articles are practical and complete. They cover app and web restore steps, edit history, how to cancel so the next payment stops, and search-term mapping for the 4,900 no-click searches.
mistake: The forecast is a single point with an optimistic currency line, not a true range. It also proposes merging the 71%-helpful 'Recording a payment' page, which is effort we don't need. The refund article's first line doesn't directly say 'go to Apple or Google'.
to10: Give the forecast as a range and drop the speculative currency and other-causes lines. Skip the payment-article merge. Lead the refund article with 'If you paid through Apple or Google, they refund it, not us.'

strength: A clear no to the 20% cut, backed by correct lifetime maths ($1,677 vs $1,130, net $1,174) and a plain break-even point of $262,500, roughly four top affiliates.
mistake: The Partner tier's 40% first-year rate raises cost for the top 20 when the complaint was payouts and lost credit, not the rate. The cost of the 90-day window is left vague ('every 10% adds $63,000') instead of being estimated.
to10: Put real dates and owners on the 30-day plan. Estimate what the 90-day window will actually cost. Reward the top tier with service and speed rather than a higher rate, or show more clearly why the extra rate is worth it.

strength: Honest, quantified decision-making. It points out that the $210k saving only exists if we cut commission on customers already earned (about $38k otherwise), projects the 90-day window cost from our own numbers, and gives a dated 30-day plan with owners.
mistake: The window projection rests on assumed 65–75% conversion by day 90 and a margin assumption, which makes it denser than grade-7 reading. The detailed legal disclosure wording runs a little heavy for a one-page rule sheet.
to10: Simplify the 'why not 20%' table into plainer words, tighten the rules page, and show a quick sensitivity check on the day-90 conversion assumption.

strength: One Monday PO table (rush, standard, re-carton) with dates and costs that add up to ₹1.187 crore, plus a dated action list and an honest gap plan: ad pause, per-shade cap, pro pre-order, real back date, no fake timers.
mistake: The run-out dates wobble: 30 Nov in the summary, 23 Nov without re-carton, and the 'sellable' count is muddled. The glitter plan is also thinner, with a price cut to ₹699 and a clearance to a buyer, but no trigger if sales miss.
to10: State plainly whether held stock is inside the 9,100 and show one clean top-5 runway. Add a sales trigger for the palette clearance, a shade-level split, and a bit more trimming to stay under 900 words.

strength: The maths is tight and shown (back-orders plus sale week at 2.5x plus buffer = 24,000 rush). The glitter plan is pragmatic: a Party pair that spares the hero shades, a marketplace floor price and a trigger.
mistake: The standard POs are placed on Fri 20 Nov for no stated reason, which splits the Monday action and delays arrival, though the plan still reaches 1 Jan. It also leans on 'reorder point' language and adds a 'bolder move' that reads like an extra option.
to10: Place every PO on Monday, or explain the delay. Add a short Tanvi-voice back-in-stock message and a rule to pause ads and cap orders on the top 5 during the gap. Cut the jargon and keep it under 900 words.

strength: Takes the 4.0 apart against the 2.5 break-even, and gives a clean split that adds to $240,000 with daily budgets and line-by-line expected results. It also adds a non-brand Search campaign for the winning themes, plus ready ad copy.
mistake: The forecast is too rosy. It assumes $18,000 of brand search returns about 25 ROAS ($455,000) and that PMax rises from about 2.0 to 2.6. That produces a 4.6 ROAS and +$60,900 profit, which is hard to trust. It also has few rules for weeks 2 to 4 beyond one reserve rule.
to10: Use a more cautious brand-value assumption and a wider profit range. Add explicit week 2 to 4 rules to scale or cut each line. Add negatives for broad and sustainable terms, and give each week-one action an owner and a done-when.

strength: A careful, honest read. It combines brand across Search and PMax, shows non-brand at 2.26 against the 2.5 break-even, and warns that reported revenue will fall while profit rises. It gives a profit range and a week-one table with owner and done-when. It also sets monthly rules for cutting and scaling.
mistake: The $104,000 reserve, 43% of budget, makes the split feel undecided, and the winning washable and work terms get no dedicated spend. The regional holdout test is complex for a small team and adds a lot of text. Some figures, such as the $61,900 feed upside, are loosely derived.
to10: Commit more of the budget to the proven winners, with a smaller reserve and a dedicated line for washable and work-comfort terms. Show expected results per line. Trim or simplify the regional test and add one line on preventing future price mismatches.

strength: It opens with what the problem costs (£139,800 in returns, £31,360 in tickets). It then gives six short one-button messages in our voice, including a post-delivery fit check for bra buyers. The work runs cheapest first, and the savings are shown as ranges with the working.
mistake: The 2-hour size-switch in the fit-check message depends on an ops capability we may not have. The swap line shows £183,800 of 'sales kept' beside real savings, which could mislead. It is also slightly over the word limit and does not say plainly that fit-finder users may differ from other buyers.
to10: Rank the three fixes by money saved in one line at the top. Say plainly that fit-finder users are self-selected, which is why it uses half the gap. Drop or de-risk the 2-hour switch. Give one realistic net £ figure for the swap change, and trim to 1,000 words.

strength: It states the decision up front. It puts a fit block in the confirmation for first-time bra buyers. It halves the fit-finder gap for self-selection, includes a hold-out and a conversion guardrail, and gives owners and dates. It also adds a bolder 'ship the swap first' idea with its risk.
mistake: It has no follow-up fit message after delivery. The day-3 message only goes out if the courier has scanned the parcel, which is thin for the silence problem. It never gives the baseline cost totals or ranks the fixes by money. It also runs over the word limit.
to10: Add a short post-delivery bra fit nudge. Show the current cost and the saving per fix in order. Make the day-3 message work with or without a scan. Trim to 1,000 words.

strength: Complete per-reason table, exact copy for every panel and outcome, correct numbers, and practical build notes including a 10% holdout test. It brings back the pause as the main save.
mistake: The money case is thin: it gives a single point estimate with no range and no first-month watch list. It also gives a 50% discount to people switching apps with no evidence it works, and its 'Pick one reason to finish' message adds a little friction.
to10: Lead with the decision and the money, give an honest range, say plainly that the pause carries almost everything, add what to watch in month one, and drop or justify the discount for switchers.

strength: It opens with the decision and the money, including a range. It warns that the pause delivers 80% of the result and that without it the flow keeps fewer people than today. It names the pause rebuild as the critical path, shows 'Cancel my subscription' in every panel, and gives a clear 'measure from day one' plan.
mistake: It offers nothing to people switching apps and gives the 'Other' group a bare exit. The reminder prompt copy is a little scripted, and it is probably over the word limit.
to10: Trim to the word limit and add a light, low-cost alternative for the 8% switching to another app. Otherwise it is already close to ready.

strength: Opens with the decision and the bad news about Apple/Google refunds, ranks by tickets removable with working, gives a forecast as a range with a clear rationale, and adds a bolder in-app line idea with risk noted.
mistake: Articles are short on platform coverage (no web steps for restore, thin refund path for splitwise.com payers) and the ticket total counts 2,900 for restore even though some are edits; also a small fumble ('Bold labels match the current app') in assumptions.
to10: Add web steps and a splitwise.com payment path, mention search-term tagging, keep the range forecast, and cut the odd assumption wording; keep the answer-first articles.

strength: Articles are fuller and more usable: web and app steps for restore, all three payment routes for Pro, cancel-subscription steps, plus the search-term tagging idea and a lower-bound sensitivity.
mistake: Forecast is a single point estimate with a stress test rather than a range, doesn't open with the headline decision, and the Simplify article has a redundant 'follow the steps above' sequence; merging Recording a payment is questionable.
to10: Lead with the decision and expected saving, give the forecast as a range up front, tighten the Simplify article steps, and keep Recording a payment as is.

strength: A dated first-30-days plan the one partner manager can run, with owners. It sits alongside lifetime maths, a clear no to the 20% cut, a one-page rules list with disclosure wording, and a perk budget for creator-educators.
mistake: Some figures are unsupported or muddled: the "$38,000 saving" and the 1,250 / 3,365 customer estimates are invented, and the break-even range mixes revenue with an assumed margin. The first-30-days table also sits oddly with the 30 Nov payout pull-forward and the 1 Jan start dates. The extra Podia-specific legal detail is useful but adds length.
to10: Drop the shaky derived numbers or show them plainly. Keep the single rate and the 90-day window, and state the cost range clearly. Tighten the word count, and make sure the first-30-days dates and the payout pull-forward line up with the January start.

strength: A straight, well-reasoned no to the 20% cut. It gives the break-even at a 12.5% revenue fall, the $1,677 vs $1,130 lifetime maths, the top-20 concentration and the rival's 40% offer, then builds a 40%-for-12-months Partner tier that rewards the top creators without raising cost across the board.
mistake: The first-30-days plan uses day ranges rather than dates. The 90-day window cost is only given as a sensitivity (about $63,000 per 10% rise) rather than a single estimate. The $46,000 cost for the 40% Partner tier applies the uplift to all of the top-20 revenue, which is rough.
to10: Give calendar dates in the 30-day plan. Add one clear total for the cost of the 90-day window plus the 40% tier. Put the lower minimum and faster payouts at the very start of the plan, and say what the $40,000 does for non-top-20 affiliates.

strength: It finds the real problem: the top 5 matte shades run out before the sale. It rushes them, orders nothing for slow lines, and comes in under ₹1.2 crore with clear unit maths and planning at 2.5 times demand for sale week.
mistake: It is harder to read. The reorder-point table and the back-order arithmetic make it dense for an ops lead. It treats the held units as already inside the 9,100 without flagging what changes if they are extra stock.
to10: Add one simple dated timeline for the ops lead. Show both readings of the held stock. Add a short customer-facing message and real shade alternatives for the gap week.

strength: The plan is clear and dated, and the ops lead can act on it Monday. It has rush and standard orders inside the cash, re-cartoning first, and honest ways to handle the 1 to 8 December gap: ad pause, order cap, pro pre-orders and a true back-in-stock message.
mistake: The held units are assumed to be inside the 9,100 rather than extra. If they are extra, the gap is smaller than shown and the orders may be too big. Selling leftover palettes to a clearance buyer at cost gives up margin.
to10: Show the top-5 cover with the held stock counted as extra, as well as inside the 9,100. Name the actual 4 foundation shades and the hero matte shades. Make the palette bundle pair with the hero lipsticks to pull traffic.

strength: It pools all brand spend and shows that non-brand Google runs at 2.26 ROAS against a 2.5 break-even, losing about $20,100. It backs this with a profit-per-segment table, a hard cut of the loss-making spend, clear rules for weeks two to four, and a day-by-day plan with owners.
mistake: Holding back $104,000 as reserve and expecting $40,000 or more of it to go unspent is very conservative. Some of the working is hard for me to follow, such as the '$59,948 ÷ 30' reasoning for changing everything at once, and the separate profit figure for the pointed flat fix. The titles and ads also use Claire's and Nina's own words less than they could.
to10: Explain the reserve logic in plainer words and use more of the customer's language in titles and ad copy. Show non-brand Performance Max on its own at 2.03, and give a short expected-profit table by line.

strength: It is the plainest to read. It isolates non-brand Performance Max at 2.03 and a $36,700 loss, and gives a budget split that adds to exactly $240,000. It sets base and cautious profit cases with numbers that check out, and its titles and ad copy use the customer's own words ('Stand All Day', 'eight hours', 'Made to Walk, Made to Wash').
mistake: It still puts $128,000 into Performance Max, which only ran at 2.03 without brand, and the base case relies on it reaching 2.6. It never says outright to block the broad 'women's flats' and 'sustainable shoes' terms. It also gives less detail than Output 1 on the cut and boost rules for weeks two to four.
to10: Add explicit negatives or caps for the broad and 'sustainable' terms in Performance Max, plus written rules for weeks two to four on what gets cut and what gets more money. It should also justify why Performance Max needs that much budget, or move more of it to the proven winners.

strength: A sharp, decisive plan with checked numbers. It openly says only half the fit-finder gap is the quiz's own effect, and it tests the change with a holdout and a 50/50 split. It adds a warning about Christmas and a bold 'ship the swap first' idea.
mistake: It never sets out what returns and tickets cost me today (£139,800 and £31,360), so I can't see the size of the prize. It also has no bra-specific fit help after delivery, only a link to the fit finder.
to10: Open with a cost baseline and rank the three fixes by money saved. Add a post-delivery fit-tips message for first-time bra buyers. Show total savings as a range.

strength: It starts with what returns and tickets cost me, then follows the cheapest-first order. The messages are warm and in our voice, and they include practical bra fit tips after delivery plus a 'how's the fit' check. The numbers table has low and high cases and a total saving.
mistake: The 2-hour size-switch in the fit-check email depends on order editing we may not have. The 'Swap my size' buttons after delivery could nudge people to send back items that fit. It also doesn't plainly say that quiz users may simply be different buyers, which would inflate the fit-finder gain.
to10: Explain the selection bias in the fit-finder numbers. Run the fit-quiz button as an A/B test with conversion as a guardrail. Soften the delivered email so its button is 'Find your fit' rather than 'Swap my size'.

strength: A complete, buildable flow. It matches an offer to each reason, splits groups by plan type and reminder status, gives the exact copy, and adds an optional 'email me in 3/6 months' for trip-over learners, which fits Greg well.
mistake: It keeps 50% off for 3 months for people switching apps, which goes against my own data on discounts. The value of that group is also loosely counted: 67 people at near full price while they are on half price.
to10: Drop the switcher discount. Put the headline numbers and the warning that the pause carries the result at the top. Give an honest range instead of single figures.

strength: Leads with the decision and the money, including a range, and flags the risk clearly. The pause does 80% of the work, and without it the flow keeps fewer people than today, so the pause is the critical path for the sprint. It also has a clear measurement plan and a smart bolder idea to prompt reminders before anyone cancels.
mistake: Trip-over learners get only a plain exit, with no 'remind me before your next trip' option. A little of the copy, such as 'It helps us help you', sounds more corporate than warm.
to10: Add the optional remind-me email for trip-over learners. Warm up the screen 1 subtitle. Show the full working for the 12-month revenue figure.

strength: It ranks the work by tickets we can actually remove and leads with the decision. It gives an honest range with clear working: 2,703 to 4,276 tickets, or $11,082 to $17,532. It also proposes a cheap in-app line for Simplify debts and sizes it.
mistake: The refund and restore articles cover only the app. There are no splitwise.com steps and no steps to cancel the subscription, so some readers will still write in. It also never suggests adding the no-click search terms to the delete article.
to10: Add web steps and cancel-subscription steps to the articles. Tag the restore article with the 4,900 no-click search phrases. Give a short outline for the currency article, since that topic has 1,800 tickets and no page.

strength: The articles are very practical. They cover iPhone, Android and web, include steps to stop the next payment, and add the no-click search phrases to the restore article. It has a clear day-by-day plan for one writer.
mistake: The forecast is one number. It also counts savings from a currency article that hasn't been written, and it plans to merge 'Recording a payment', which already helps 71% of readers and doesn't need it. There's no summary up top telling me the decision.
to10: Give the forecast as a range, and leave out pages that aren't written yet or show them separately. Drop the unnecessary merge. Open with a two-line summary of what to do and what it saves.

strength: A clear no on the 20% cut, backed by correct lifetime maths ($1,677 against $1,130, and $1,174 kept after commission), the break-even point and the risk of losing just 4 of the top 20.
mistake: The Partner tier pays 40% for the first year. That raises the rate, matches the rival on price instead of fixing what partners complained about, and the cost of the 90-day window is left vague.
to10: Keep the rate flat and reward the top tier with service instead. Put a real cost on the 90-day window, and give the first 30 days actual dates and owners.

strength: It says plainly that the plan costs more, not $210,000 less, and gives a costed range for the 90-day window. It also shows that cutting only new referrals saves just about $38,000. The tiers reward the top partners with faster pay and service, not a higher rate.
mistake: A few parts read above grade 7, such as the projection maths and the rel="sponsored" note. Some estimates, like the $38,000 and the 65–75% credited by day 90, rest on assumptions that are stated but not proven.
to10: Simplify the wording to suit our reading level. Show the working behind the $38,000 figure in one line, and confirm it fits the word limit.

strength: The rush and standard orders for the top 5 shades, with unit costs and arrival dates, fit inside the cash. It also covers the stock-out gap with honest back-orders and a pro pre-book, and has a clear glitter and liquid plan.
mistake: It is dense and jargon-heavy ('reorder point', long maths paragraphs), which is hard for an ops lead to act on. It also holds the standard orders to Friday for no reason, and it treats the held 3,900 as already inside the 9,100, so it misses the 13,000 / 3.4 weeks / roughly 8 December outcome.
to10: Place every order on Monday, plainly, and make the re-cartoning step the headline task. State the top-5 stock as 13,000 after re-cartoning, if that is what the data means. Cut it to under 900 words with a simple date list, and add a short back-in-stock message in brand voice.

strength: It is one clean plan for Monday, with every order placed that day, a dated action table for the ops lead, and plain language. It protects both Tanvi and Farah honestly, with a real restock date, a notify button, a pro pre-order and no fake scarcity.
mistake: It also treats the held units as inside the 9,100, so it plans for a stock-out and misses the longer cover after re-cartoning. The glitter clearance is thin: selling leftovers 'at no less than cost' to a buyer who may not exist, with no real cash target.
to10: Treat the re-cartoned top-5 stock as 13,000 and restate the stock-out date. Give a firmer glitter cash-recovery target and channel. Add a short on-brand back-in-stock message and tighten the ad pause and order cap.

strength: It takes the 4.0 apart against the 2.5 break-even and shows profit by segment. Non-brand comes out at 2.26 and about -$20,100, so the cause of my profit problem is plain. The $240,000 split adds up, with explicit negatives, week-two-to-four rules and an honest forecast that revenue falls but profit rises, as a range.
mistake: It is dense and a bit over-engineered for a grade-7 brand. A $104,000 reserve with an expected $40,000 or more unspent, plus a regional holdout test, makes the plan harder to act on. It also runs a little long.
to10: Trim to the word limit, drop or simplify the geo test, shrink the reserve into firmer line items, and add a few ad lines in our voice. Then I could hand it straight to the team.

strength: It is clean and easy to read. The break-even table by campaign is correct and the price-mismatch diagnosis is practical. The titles and the search headlines in our voice ('Made to Walk, Made to Wash') are ready to use, and it cautions to claim 'folds flat' only where true.
mistake: The forecast is not believable. Brand search at $18,000 returns ROAS 25 and $455,000 of value, and total value rises to $1.11M even though PMax is cut by $82,000. A CFO would not trust a plan that promises more revenue from less spend. It also never says plainly to cut the broad 'women's flats' spend, and gives little guidance for weeks two to four.
to10: Rebuild the forecast on realistic brand value, with a profit range that does not rely on brand search growing. Add explicit negatives or caps for the 1.2 and 1.6 segments, and clear week-two-to-four rules for what gets more money and what gets cut.

strength: The opening decision with its three fixes in order is crisp. It adds a holdout, a conversion guardrail, a Christmas warning and a halved fit-finder effect, so the numbers read as honest ranges.
mistake: It never states the baseline cost of returns (£139,800) or the cost of all tickets, and it doesn't rank the fixes by money saved. It also gives only one post-delivery message, and the sales-kept figures ignore that a swap still costs £7.50 in postage.
to10: Show a clear baseline cost and a ranked table of savings with a total in pounds. Add a dedicated fit-help follow-up for first-time bra buyers. Net the swap postage cost out of the sales-kept claim.

strength: It opens with the cost baseline and the key facts, all correct: £139,800, 5,394 too-small returns and 6,076 day 3 to 5 tickets. Its six messages are warm and on brand, including the fit-help follow-up and "Comfort beats the number on the tag". The table of numbers is easy to check and states its assumptions.
mistake: The fit-check email 10 minutes after ordering promises a free size switch within 2 hours. That depends on an ops capability we may not have. The £183,800 sales-kept figure is a big ceiling that is flagged but not netted out of the total.
to10: Drop the 2-hour switch promise or make it an optional extra. Show the swap value in a realistic range inside the total saved. Add a fit-finder placement test with a guardrail on bra conversion.

strength: A full set of screens for every reason with warm copy, including a 'remind me when the next trip comes up' option. Good build notes and a 10% holdout test.
mistake: The money section has loose spots. The £607 'after discount' line for the app switchers doesn't match the maths. It gives a single figure with no range for rates that are mostly guesses. It also invents a 12% / 4% split for 'not making progress' and keeps a discount for switchers with no evidence it works.
to10: State a range, fix the switcher line, and say plainly that the pause carries almost all the result. Add what to watch in the first month and a clear build order.

strength: It leads with the decision and the money, and the numbers tie out (842 vs 2,210, £18,650 a month, £29,160 of discounts ended). It also says honestly that the pause does 80% of the work and that without it the flow is worse than today. It gives a range and tells us what to measure.
mistake: The build plan is thin beyond 'rebuild the pause first'. The 'bolder move' section goes beyond the brief. Panels for switchers and 'Other' are bare, with no offer at all.
to10: A short sprint order, and a light touch for app switchers such as a pause or a reminder. Cut the extra section or shrink it to make room.

strength: It rewrites "How balances work" under Jordan's own question, ranks the fixes by tickets we can remove, and the Pro article covers refunds and how to cancel. The forecast shows its working and adds a lower-end case.
mistake: The delete article is titled "How to undo a deleted expense" and does not use the searched words "restore" or "recover". The Simplify article has a clumsy "Follow the steps above" step. The forecast is a single point estimate with only a halved fallback, and the plan to merge "Recording a payment" into a new article is weak.
to10: Put the searched phrases in the delete article's title. Fix the repeated-steps wording in article 1. Give a proper range instead of a point estimate. Drop the unneeded merge. Add a settle-up link and a firmer plan for the currency gap.

strength: It opens with the decision, the bad news about store refunds and its assumptions. The delete article is titled "Undo delete: restore a deleted expense", in the words people search. The forecast is a range with a source for each share, the arithmetic checks out, and it adds an optional in-app line on the balances screen.
mistake: It writes a new Simplify article instead of rewriting "How balances work" itself, so the old page stays only partly fixed. Article 1 states flatly that the group has Simplify debts on, which will be wrong for some readers. The Pro article does not give cancel steps.
to10: Soften the opening line of the Simplify article to "probably". Rewrite the old balances article, not just add a pointer to it. Add cancel steps to the Pro article. Include the week-2 currency article in the forecast.

strength: A straight no to the 20% cut, with the lifetime maths and the break-even in top-20 partners. It also gives a dated first-30-days plan the one partner manager can run, and strong disclosure rules with real-world specifics (US/UK).
mistake: Some numbers are shaky or unexplained: the $38,000 'cut only new referrals' saving, the 1,250 new referred customers from '3,365 x 3.1% x 12', and the $62-89k window cost rest on assumed pay-by-day-90 rates. The break-even range mixes revenue and margin assumptions. The 'pay October with September' step is also a confusing way to pull payouts forward.
to10: Show the derivation of each projection plainly, drop the muddled break-even range, and state the net effect of the whole plan against finance's $210k in one line. Keep the dated 30-day plan and the bolder 'Who sent you?' idea.

strength: A clear 'do not cut' answer with the lifetime maths (referred $1,677, net $1,174, others $1,130), the 12.5% break-even, and a sensible mid-tier of active affiliates. The rules are short and on voice.
mistake: Tiering Partners to 40% for the first 12 months raises cost on a rule the brief wanted to avoid, and the cost math is muddled: '10 points on 31% of $1.49M' undercounts, and the '4 can wipe it out' claim is hand-wavy. The 30-day plan has no calendar dates. The $100 first-customer bonus could drift toward an earnings promise.
to10: Give calendar dates and a clearer total cost against the $210k. Tighten the cost lines, and justify the 40% tier or drop it. Add more on how the partner manager handles the load.

strength: One decisive Monday plan inside the cash. The rush order (22,000 at ₹207, lands 7 Dec) plus the January standard order total ₹1.187 crore, the sums check out, and the dated ops table runs straight through the sale.
mistake: Foundation goes to only 4 of 20 shades. The other 16 could run short in January with no mitigation named. The order cap of 4 per shade could also frustrate pros outside the pre-order.
to10: Add a plan for the 16 foundation shades left out and show the rush-quantity working line by line. Also name the specific alternative shades for customers who find their hero shade out.

strength: The working is shown and checks out. The rush quantity (3,300 + 16,965 + buffer = 24,000), the 82% versus 42% critique of the draft and the palette cost maths are all right. It adds an honest back-order flow, trigger-based Monday checks and a costed palette clearance with a floor.
mistake: It contains small errors. Foundation and kohl actually hit their reorder points around 5 Dec, not 25 Nov, and 'all lines last to about 12 Feb' doesn't match its own 7 Feb top-5 maths. The standard POs are delayed to 20 Nov for no stated reason, and the pre-book is framed as an optional 'bolder move'.
to10: Fix the reorder-date and runout claims and place the standard POs Monday. Fold the pro pre-book into the core plan and tighten the dense maths paragraphs for the ops lead.

strength: It splits the 4.0 into brand and non-brand ($479,520 on $26,700 versus 2.26 ROAS on everything else) and gives profit after ads for every segment. Every number checks out. The budget and the $146,300 of cuts add to exactly $240,000, with clear weekly rules for scaling and cutting.
mistake: Holding $104,000 in reserve and adding a regional geo test makes the month more complex than most teams can run. A 'products only' Performance Max with video paused is also harder to set up than the plan suggests.
to10: Cut the reserve to a planned, smaller amount and give an expected value per line, as Output 2 does. Add ready-to-use ad and asset copy in the brand voice, and say what to check so price mismatches don't return after a sale.

strength: The profit table is clean, and the base and cautious forecasts add up to the dollar. The feed fix steps are concrete (sale_price, automatic item updates, check five variants). The headlines and titles use Claire's and Nina's own words in the brand voice.
mistake: It keeps $128,000 in Performance Max with no negatives on broad 'women's flats' or 'sustainable shoes', so most of the money-losing spend survives. Its own cautious case has Performance Max at 2.2 ROAS, which is below break-even.
to10: Explicitly exclude or cap the broad and sustainable terms and display spend. Shrink Performance Max to the proven themes plus the restored pointed flat sizes. Add rules for weeks two to four on what to cut when a line sits below 2.5.

strength: A tight executive summary with weekly and monthly ranges that check out (762 tickets a week down to 478 to 573; bra returns 31% down to 27.3% to 28.6%). It treats fit-finder selection bias honestly by counting only half the 19-point gap and testing on half of traffic.
mistake: It assumes calendar dates in November and December and a Christmas peak that the brief never mentions. It also has no fit-help message after delivery beyond a quiz link, and it claims that showing a delivery range will cut 'arrived too late' returns, which it does not support.
to10: Add bra fit tips in a post-delivery check-in, rank the three fixes by pounds saved with a total, and drop the invented calendar dates.

strength: It covers what I asked for and its numbers reconcile: the £139,800 returns and £31,360 tickets baseline, 6,076 tickets on days 3 to 5, the 5,394 and 1,767 size returns, a summed £11.8k to £19.8k saving, and 117 tickets per 1,000 orders. It also adds a fit check before dispatch and real bra fit tips plus a check-in after delivery.
mistake: 'We're packing your order now' and the two-hour size switch both depend on operations that may not exist. The delivered email leads with 'Swap my size', which nudges people towards a return before they've tried it.
to10: Make the delivered email's button 'Find your fit' rather than swap, confirm the switch-before-picking window with the warehouse, and state per-week ticket targets for the hold-out read.

strength: The numbers all check: 2,210 kept, £18,650 a month, 440 without the pause, and £29,160 of discounts ended. It warns plainly that the pause does 80% of the work and must not launch without it, and it gives a range.
mistake: The 'trip over' group gets only a plain exit. There is no 'remind me before your next trip' or pause option, so Greg's 'maybe next spring' goes unused. The 12-month revenue figure also rests on a 6% churn assumption that is only loosely explained.
to10: Add an opt-in 'email me before my next trip' line for goal or trip cancellers. Add a holdout group on today's flow to prove the gain. Show the 12-month revenue working in one line.

strength: Each reason gets the right offer, including a 'remind me in 3 or 6 months' checkbox for trip-over cancellers and a smaller-goal option for people who already have a reminder. It adds a sensible 10% holdout on today's flow, and the main maths is correct (1,771 pause, 304 switch, 2,239 total).
mistake: It keeps the 50% off for switchers based on an assumed rate, when we know 61% of discount takers leave anyway. It gives no range. The £136k a year assumes zero churn, and the £9 monthly price used for £59.40 is a guess shown as if it were fact.
to10: Drop the discount for switchers or test it in the holdout. Give an honest range. Add churn to the yearly figure. Set out the build steps in order, with the pause as the critical path.

strength: Three answer-first articles in our voice. Article 1 hedges with 'probably' for the 37% of balance cases that aren't Simplify debts, and article 3 adds how to cancel Pro. The forecast arithmetic checks out (3,743 tickets, about $15,300), and it adds the deleted-expense search terms as a cheap extra fix.
mistake: It proposes merging 'Recording a payment', which already helps 71% of readers, for little gain. It counts all 2,900 deleted-or-edited tickets at 40% without separating edits from deletes. The headline forecast is a single point estimate, with a range added only afterwards by halving the shares.
to10: Drop the payment-article merge and use the in-app link to fix its reach instead. Lead with a short decision summary. Give the forecast as a range per topic from the start.

strength: It opens with the decision and the bad news about Apple and Google refunds. Every forecast row is a range, and the totals all check out: 7,861 tickets in reach, 2,703 to 4,276 fewer, $11,082 to $17,532 saved. It sensibly leaves the 71% payment article alone and fixes its reach with a link. The costed bolder idea of a Simplify debts banner is a good addition.
mistake: Article 1 states flatly 'Your group has Simplify debts turned on', but that is true for only 63% of balance tickets, so it misleads the rest. The refund article tells people to cancel but doesn't give the steps.
to10: Soften the first line of article 1 to 'probably' or 'if'. Add the cancel steps for each store to the refund article. Add the failed search terms as synonyms on the restore article.

strength: It gives a straight no on the 20% cut and backs it with correct lifetime maths ($1,677 vs $1,130, $1,174 net), a break-even range and a top-20 loss count. It also sizes the 90-day window cost from the real customer base (3,365 customers, about 1,250 new a year).
mistake: The window-cost projection rests on an assumed 65–75% pay-by-day-90 curve. It also includes legal disclosure claims ("affiliate link alone is not enough" in the US) that a lawyer should check before partners see them.
to10: Show a sensitivity check on the 90-day uplift, and add a measure of whether partner tier status actually changes partner behaviour, beyond faster payouts. Tighten the wording toward grade 7 in the tables.

strength: The case against the cut is clean and well argued: a 12.5% break-even, four top partners able to wipe out the saving, and first-year commission compared against the rival's 40%. It also matches the rival directly for the core partners.
mistake: It adds a 40% first-year rate (about $46k) and a first-customer bonus. Both raise cost and spend perk money away from the top 20. The window cost is left vague ('every 10% adds $63k'), and the 30-day plan has no real dates.
to10: Put a number on the 90-day window cost. Justify the 40% partner rate against keeping the cost flat, or drop it. Put calendar dates on the 30-day plan.

strength: It puts the cash where it matters: rush and standard orders for the top 5 matte shades, no money wasted on liquid or glitter, and a practical plan to move dead palette stock.
mistake: It mishandles the re-cartoning math. Re-cartoning the 3,900 top-5 held units should lift top-5 stock to about 13,000 units and carry us to the rush delivery; the plan instead creates an unnecessary 1 to 7 December stockout/back-order gap.
to10: Fix the held-stock assumption and remove the false stockout plan, make the Monday PO dates fully consistent, and show the top-5 shade split clearly enough for ops to place the POs without interpretation.

strength: It is very easy to act on: one Monday order table, clear dates, cash inside budget, and the right call to reject the ₹1.86 crore draft.
mistake: It assumes the 3,900 held top-5 units are inside the 9,100 on hand, so it creates a false sellout gap and recommends pausing ads and capping orders when re-cartoning should largely prevent the gap.
to10: Correct the held-stock math, show that re-cartoning gets us to the rush arrival, avoid unnecessary demand suppression, and sharpen the customer-facing copy into a bolder SUGAR voice.

strength: It takes apart the blended 4.0 ROAS properly, shows brand is hiding weak non-brand performance, calculates profit after ad spend, and puts the price-mismatch feed issue first.
mistake: The budget plan is overcomplicated and not fully comfortable to act on: a very large reserve, likely unspent budget, a regional test, and some questionable PMax setup language make it less ready than it first looks.
to10: A cleaner $240,000 allocation with less reserve, clearer expected results by line, and more practical PMax controls focused on washable, standing-all-day, and bags without the extra geo test.

strength: It gives me the main owner answer clearly: break-even is 2.5, PMax without brand loses money, bags and washable/comfort terms deserve money, and the pointed-flat feed problem is the first fix.
mistake: The forecast is a little optimistic, especially assuming brand search can absorb nearly all PMax brand value at a much higher ROAS and that brand search will run around 25 ROAS.
to10: Tighten the forecast assumptions, show a slightly more conservative PMax non-brand plan, and spell out how PMax will be constrained away from broad flats, sustainable, display, and video waste.

strength: It finds the real levers in the data, ranks them well, and gives believable ranges with the working shown.
mistake: The day-3 message only goes to scanned parcels, so it may miss some of the silence that is creating WISMO tickets; I would tighten that trigger.
to10: Add a clearer day-3 no-scan customer message/escalation, remove the dated Christmas/November assumptions unless confirmed, and include one more bra-specific post-delivery fit nudge.

strength: Very practical and complete: it covers the messages, portal, fit quiz placement, rollout order, holdout, and numbers cleanly.
mistake: It adds an assumed 2-hour size-change window and a few extra touches without proving they are feasible, and some copy is a little less on-brand than Output 1.
to10: Make the operational assumptions lighter, sharpen the brand language around bra fit, and rank the expected value of the three fixes more explicitly.

strength: It finds the main lever in the data, makes the pause the critical path, stops wasting discounts on trip-over customers, and gives product a buildable one-screen flow with usable copy.
mistake: The forecast slightly overreaches on the untested reminder/plan-switch assumptions and appears to count all not-progress cancellers in the reminder estimate, not just the 72% without reminders.
to10: Tighten the maths by reason, separate proven from assumed uplift, and make the revenue table fully auditable line by line.

strength: It is clear, practical, and gets the big ideas right: bring back pause, use the annual plan for price objections, and use reminders for progress problems.
mistake: It keeps the 50% discount for switchers without evidence, which is exactly the sort of margin leak this new flow should avoid; it also muddles the required reason with an 'always live' cancel button.
to10: Remove the unsupported discount, make every reason panel visibly include the cancel button, and clean up the assumptions so the forecast is less optimistic and easier to trust.

strength: It goes straight at the three biggest removable causes, uses the customer’s own search words, writes the articles in a calm plain voice, and shows its ticket-saving math.
mistake: It suggests merging the already-helpful payment article and counts some currency benefit without actually writing that article; I would also verify every restore/refund button label before publishing.
to10: Make the forecast a range first, leave the payment article alone unless evidence says otherwise, verify the product steps, and add at least a short currency article outline for week 2.

strength: The prioritisation and forecast are disciplined: it ranks by tickets we can remove, gives a sensible range, and does not overcount the week-2 work.
mistake: The balance article is too certain that Simplify debts is the cause, and a few article steps are less complete or slightly risky, especially refund cancellation and deleted-expense recovery.
to10: Soften the balance answer to 'probably', add fuller Apple/Google cancellation steps, include web recovery steps, add search synonyms explicitly, and make the in-app Simplify debts message part of the main plan rather than a bolder extra.

strength: It makes the right call immediately: do not cut to 20%, fix credit and payouts, and spend the partner manager’s time on the top creator-educators.
mistake: Some of the projected cost maths for the 90-day window is a bit too confident from the data given, and the date-specific 30-day plan would need checking before sending.
to10: Tighten the assumptions behind the extra commission forecast, remove any speculative numbers that cannot be defended, and make the rollout dates generic or confirmed.

strength: It clearly explains why the 20% cut is risky, using the break-even revenue drop, top-20 concentration, churn, and lifetime value in a way finance would understand.
mistake: The 40% first-year Partner tier adds cost and complexity when the data says the real problems are lost credit and slow payouts, not the headline rate.
to10: Keep 30% for both tiers, use the tier for service and payout advantages instead of a higher commission, and sharpen the cost forecast for the new 90-day window.

strength: It spots the real problem fast: the top 5 matte shades, not the whole matte line, and turns that into a cash-feasible action plan with dates and line-by-line orders.
mistake: It says the one-week top-5 gap cannot be closed, but its own timing is a bit loose and it leans on a 28 Dec arrival date that should be stated more carefully against the 42-day lead time.
to10: Tighten the date math, show the rush and standard quantities by each of the 5 hero shades, and make the December gap plan operationally cleaner across D2C, marketplaces and retail allocation.

strength: It reads like an owner-ready operating plan: it uses the right constraint, puts re-cartoning first, protects the hero shades, keeps inside cash, and handles the stock gap honestly.
mistake: It adds a few extra frameworks and ideas that are useful but slightly more than the brief asked for, and the 1 Jan standard-arrival date should be checked carefully against exact PO timing.
to10: Give the exact unit split for each hero shade, tighten the arrival-date math, and turn the back-order and channel-allocation rules into a single execution table the ops team can follow without interpretation.

strength: It gets to the core issue fast: PMax is being flattered by brand, non-brand PMax is below break-even, and the feed disapproval on pointed flats is the first thing to fix.
mistake: The reallocation and forecast lean optimistic in places, especially the very strong brand-search uplift and some assumed ROAS gains from the new mix without enough caution on how fast those gains will show up.
to10: Tighten the forecast assumptions, make the budget deployment rules a bit more explicit for weeks 2 to 4, and ground the expected results in a clearer base/cautious scenario tied to the exact campaigns being scaled.

strength: It thinks like an owner on profit, not vanity ROAS, and it introduces useful control rules and a disciplined reserve approach instead of spending the full budget just because it is available.
mistake: It overreaches operationally and technically in ways that make it less usable right now, including claims about PMax negatives/products-only behavior and a plan that effectively assumes large under-spend against a brief that asked how to split the full $240,000 next month.
to10: Keep the profit-first framing, but simplify it into a cleaner 30-day plan with fully reliable Google Ads mechanics, a crisper exact budget allocation, and fewer side experiments competing with the urgent feed and spend fixes.

strength: It finds the three real levers in our data, puts them in the right order, and gives me usable copy plus a sensible test-and-holdout plan.
mistake: It overstates some financial upside, especially the swap revenue line, and one message rule is bent by swapping the CTA in the order confirmation for bra buyers instead of keeping the core order button.
to10: Tighten the revenue math on exchanges, keep one consistent owner-friendly KPI table, and make the first-bra order confirmation answer both questions at once: order received and fit help.

strength: It is practical and balanced: strong message set, good portal changes, and it catches the key point that our silence between warehouse exit and courier scan is creating tickets.
mistake: It slips beyond post-purchase into a pre-purchase site change and adds assumptions like a 2-hour size-switch window that may not be operationally true for us.
to10: Keep the same structure but anchor every recommendation more tightly to our actual flow, trim speculative steps, and sharpen the expected impact with more conservative, better-explained maths.

strength: It gives me a buildable one-screen flow with reason-matched offers, exact copy, and it correctly brings back the pause as the main save.
mistake: It spends a 50% discount on 'switching apps' with no evidence that this is the right group, and some of the math and assumptions around kept value are a bit too loose for me to sign off unchanged.
to10: Tighten the revenue model by separating 90-day retained subs from immediate monthly revenue, drop the unsupported discount for switching-app users, and add a simple first-month success metric table with target thresholds.

strength: It thinks like an owner: it puts the pause rebuild first, stops blanket discounting, and explicitly warns me not to launch without the one proven save.
mistake: It leaves some value on the table by giving no tested save to switching-app users and its forward revenue maths and discount-savings lines are a bit overreaching for the evidence provided.
to10: Add slightly tighter quantified assumptions for the annual-plan and reminder saves, clean up the revenue framing, and include exact copy for the reminder-already-set variant and the optional return reminder for trip-finished users.

strength: It ranks the work by likely ticket reduction, spots the Simplify debts and app-store refund issues clearly, and gives a sensible ticket-savings range with working.
mistake: It invents product details that are not in the brief, especially restoring deleted expenses from Activity and turning off Simplify debts to see pairwise debts; if those steps are wrong, the article is risky to publish.
to10: Keep the prioritisation and forecast, but remove unverified product behavior, tighten the copy to only confirmed steps, and include the currency article plan without overreaching on UI behavior.

strength: It understands the main business levers, writes in a friendly plain voice, and connects search intent and in-app links to likely ticket reduction.
mistake: It makes more unsupported product claims than output 1, especially around undelete/history behavior, web steps, refund flows, and merging 'Recording a payment' into 'Settle up' despite the article already performing well.
to10: Re-rank the work around highest removable tickets, stop inventing unverified product steps, keep 'Recording a payment' separate, and make the forecast more evidence-led and conservative.

strength: It makes the right core call with the right math: keep 30%, focus on the top partners, extend credit, and fix payouts in a way that fits our actual bottlenecks.
mistake: The proposed 40% first-year Partner tier is directionally smart but a bit too expensive and more complex than needed for a one-manager team, especially when our own data says payout speed and credit loss are the main complaints.
to10: Keep the same strategic spine, but tighten the cost of the top tier, make the credited-revenue upside and downside a little more explicit, and simplify execution so one partner manager can run it without strain.

strength: It understands that the real problems are under-crediting and payout friction, not the headline commission rate, and it puts attention on the top creator-educators where it belongs.
mistake: It introduces shakier assumptions and extra complexity, especially the projected customer counts and the 'Who sent you?' credit idea, which creates dispute risk and is not something I would roll out from this draft.
to10: Use cleaner, more defensible math from the data we actually have, drop speculative mechanisms, and turn it into a simpler operating plan I could hand to one partner manager tomorrow.

strength: It focuses cash on the real risk: the top 5 matte shades, starts re-cartoning immediately, rejects the over-budget draft, and gives ops a dated action plan.
mistake: It treats the held crushed-carton stock a bit inconsistently and creates a 1–8 Dec stockout gap that may not exist if the 3,900 top-5 held units are added to the 9,100 on hand.
to10: Fix the held-stock assumption, recalculate the top-5 runout date, and tighten the palette clearance plan with a clearer sell-through target and channel owner.

strength: The order quantities are tight, cash-aware, and well reasoned, with a useful pro pre-book idea for bridal artists.
mistake: It says the top 5 still have only 2.4 weeks after re-cartoning, which misses the main warehouse fix and leads to an unnecessary back-order gap.
to10: Correct the re-cartoning math, place all POs on Monday rather than some by Friday, and make the slow-stock plan more decisive for turning glitter inventory into cash.

strength: It clearly exposes the real issue: brand is hiding weak non-brand PMax performance, and it translates ROAS into actual profit after ad spend.
mistake: The plan holds back $104,000 and expects some budget to stay unspent, which clashes with the request for a $240,000 next-month split; the campaign setup also gets a bit too complex with the regional test.
to10: Make the budget plan simpler and fully operational against the $240,000 ceiling, clean up the daily budget math, and put the feed fix and budget reallocation into a tighter week-one plan without the extra geo test unless it is clearly optional.

strength: It is practical, clear, and ordered correctly: fix the disapproved pointed flats first, exclude brand from PMax, fund bags and high-intent washable/comfort demand, and judge everything against 2.5 break-even ROAS.
mistake: The expected results are a little optimistic, especially assuming brand search can absorb almost all PMax brand value at a much higher ROAS and that brand-excluded PMax can quickly improve from 2.03 to 2.6.
to10: Make the forecast more conservative, show the math for the expected brand transfer more carefully, and add firmer cut rules for PMax sub-themes after the first two weeks.

strength: It finds the real levers: courier silence, bra fit, and the refund-biased portal, then gives usable copy, sequencing, and sensible ranges with the maths shown.
mistake: The exchange sales-kept number is a ceiling and could be read too confidently; I would label it more clearly as retained revenue at risk, not cost saving.
to10: Tighten the revenue assumptions for swaps, add a clearer holdout/test plan by channel, and make sure the day-3 message handles no-scan parcels as well as scanned ones.

strength: It is sharp on the main decision and gives honest, useful targets, especially by assuming only half the fit-finder gap is caused by the quiz.
mistake: The day-3 update misses part of the main WISMO problem: if there is no courier scan by day 3, it sends the warehouse to check but does not clearly reassure the customer proactively.
to10: Add a proactive no-scan customer message, include a post-delivery bra fit/swap nudge, remove the unnecessary Christmas/date assumptions, and make the delivered CTA point more directly to swapping when fit is wrong.

strength: It gives the product team a buildable one-screen flow with exact copy, clear reason-by-reason treatments, and mostly sound subscriber maths.
mistake: The 50% discount for people switching apps is assumed rather than proven, and the revenue treatment around discounted users is a little too neat.
to10: Make the pause the explicit critical path, tighten the discounted-revenue maths, and be clearer that untested offers need a holdout before we trust the projections.

strength: It puts the most important decision first: rebuild the pause or do not launch, because that is where almost all the value is.
mistake: It is a bit light on tailored save options for some groups, especially switching apps and learners who already have reminders, and the 12-month revenue numbers could show more working.
to10: Add slightly warmer customer copy, show the full annual-plan price math in the screen text, and spell out the first-year revenue calculation so finance can trust it immediately.

strength: It finds the biggest preventable causes, writes the three most useful articles in our voice, and gives a sensible ticket-saving range with clear working.
mistake: A few article steps and labels would need a product check before publishing, especially the exact paths for settings and store refunds.
to10: Tighten the articles after checking exact app labels on iOS, Android and web, and make the Simplify debts article the main rewrite of the existing balance page rather than only a new linked page.

strength: It is practical, clear, and puts the Simplify debts, deleted expense, and app-store refund problems near the top with usable draft articles.
mistake: It overpromises in places, especially 'nothing is lost for good,' and it misses the Settle up help link even though that is a large ticket area with an already helpful article.
to10: Remove the overclaim about history, verify the web and refund steps, add the Settle up in-app link, and give an honest range rather than mainly one point estimate.

strength: It makes the right strategic call: do not cut to 20%, because referred customers are better customers and the real problems are lost credit, slow payouts, and the top 20 partners feeling ignored.
mistake: Some of the projection math around the 90-day window and the year-one savings from cutting only new referrals is a bit hand-wavy and would need finance to check before we publish it internally.
to10: Tighten the cost model for the 90-day window, simplify a few numbers, and turn the first-30-days table into the exact operating checklist for the partner manager.

strength: It is very clear and gets the main answer right: the 20% cut is risky, the top 20 matter most, and the 30-day credit window is unfair to partners like Kwame.
mistake: It adds a 40% first-year Partner tier even though the data says payout speed and attribution are the real complaints, and the cost estimate for that tier is not strong enough for a finance conversation.
to10: Keep the 30% rate, make the Partner tier about service, speed, attribution, and co-marketing, and sharpen the cost controls around the bonus and free account ideas.

strength: It spots the real issue fast: hero matte shades will run out before the sale, and it uses the crushed-carton stock plus rush ordering instead of wasting cash on slow lines.
mistake: The key math is shaky in places, especially saying top-5 stock is still only 2.4 weeks after re-cartoning and relying on a back-order gap that the recartoned units should mostly close; that makes me question the exact order quantities and dates.
to10: Tighten the stock-flow math around the top 5 shades, remove contradictions, and give fully reliable arrival and coverage calculations I can hand straight to ops without checking.

strength: It gives me one cash-aware action plan that matches the real business risk: protect the top 5 matte shades for weddings and the sale, stop ordering overstocked lines, and turn slow stock into cash.
mistake: The top-5 gap handling is a bit too accepting of a stockout window instead of pushing harder on whether recartoned stock plus demand controls can reduce or avoid it, and a few date/details could be tightened.
to10: Make the top-5 stock timing airtight to the day, sharpen the exact shade splits and customer message, and confirm the clearance pricing logic so I could publish it internally unchanged.

strength: It gets to the real issue fast: Performance Max looks good only because brand is mixed in, and it puts the feed disapproval problem first where it belongs.
mistake: The reallocation is a bit too optimistic and not fully grounded in channels we know we can actually control, especially the expected jump in brand search value and the new non-brand search line.
to10: Tighten the forecast assumptions, make the $240,000 plan more operationally certain, and be a little more careful on what PMax can and cannot do with exclusions and asset control.

strength: It challenges the headline 4.0 ROAS, explains profit clearly, and adds a disciplined reserve rule instead of forcing spend just because budget exists.
mistake: It includes several recommendations that are not reliable or not clearly feasible in this setup, like some PMax controls and the large holdback plan, and a few calculations/claims overreach the evidence.
to10: Keep the profit-first framing but replace the speculative mechanics with a practical spend plan that uses the full budget intentionally, fixes the feed first, and sticks to changes we can confidently implement in Google Ads and Merchant Center.

strength: It focuses on the three real levers in this business, ranks them well, writes usable message copy, and gives measured ranges instead of pretending the uplift is certain.
mistake: It slightly muddles the day-3 update logic versus the owner's likely fix, and its kept-sales maths is presented a bit too boldly for what is really a ceiling.
to10: Tighten the operational logic on the proactive shipping updates, make the financial impact on swaps more conservative and explicit, and add a little more clarity on how success will be measured by segment.

strength: It understands the business problem well, adds a smart post-delivery bra fit flow, and keeps the refund option visible while pushing size swaps in a customer-friendly way.
mistake: A few assumptions and numbers stretch beyond the brief, especially the aggressive swap-value calculation and operational details like the 2-hour size-change window that are not grounded in the data provided.
to10: Anchor every projected number more tightly to the given data, remove unsupported operational assumptions, and separate cost savings from revenue retained more carefully.

strength: It spots the core business truth fast: the pause is the main win, one offer for everyone wastes money, and the flow should be reason-matched with cancel always visible.
mistake: A few revenue assumptions are a bit shaky or under-explained, especially the 12-month value math and the longer-term revenue framing.
to10: Tighten the financial model so every number is fully traceable by reason and plan, and add a very explicit build order checklist for the sprint.

strength: It is easy to read and gives a buildable one-screen flow with solid copy and a clear structure for the team.
mistake: It keeps a 50% discount for people switching apps without evidence, and some numbers and assumptions are off or too loose for me to trust the business case.
to10: Drop unsupported discounting, align every offer tightly to the data we actually have, and make the retention and revenue math fully reliable.

strength: It prioritises the biggest preventable causes using the business data, writes publishable articles in the right voice, and gives a cautious forecast with working.
mistake: It says nothing needs merging even though the brief asked what to fix, merge or write first, and it adds a product-change suggestion that goes beyond the stated one-day link change.
to10: Tighten a few facts and assumptions in the article steps, cover merge/fix decisions a bit more explicitly, and keep the scope strictly to what the brief asked for.

strength: It covers the right problem areas, includes useful search-term and in-app-link ideas, and the structure is easy to follow.
mistake: Several article details overreach or are likely inaccurate from the data given, especially around undelete/history and the exact refund flows, so I would not publish it without checking product facts.
to10: Be more disciplined about only claiming steps and product behaviour we know, keep the plan tighter around highest-impact changes first, and make the forecast depend less on extra work not clearly in scope.

strength: It gives one clear plan built around our actual economics: keep 30%, fix the 30-day window and payouts, and focus the programme on the top creator-educators who already drive most revenue.
mistake: The proposed 40% first-year Partner tier likely blows past the stated $40,000 perks budget and raises programme cost more than the plan fully reconciles, especially on top of a 90-day window.
to10: Keep the same sharp argument against the 20% cut, but tighten the cost model so the top-tier benefits stay within a clearly bounded budget and operating load for one partner manager.

strength: It surfaces an important idea beyond the obvious fixes: the programme is under-crediting creator influence, and the test of survey-based attribution could help recover missed partner value.
mistake: It makes too many shaky assumptions and introduces unnecessary specificity that is hard to trust, including questionable maths around new-customer volumes and some legal/compliance claims that go beyond the brief.
to10: Simplify it to the strongest core plan, remove speculative numbers and legal flourishes, and make the economics watertight around LTV, the 90-day window and partner focus.

strength: It focuses the cash where the real risk is: top 5 matte shades, re-cartoning first, no orders for liquid or glitter, and a clear Monday action plan inside ₹1.2 crore.
mistake: It is inconsistent on the held top-5 stock and creates a 1-8 December stockout gap that should mostly be avoided once the 3,900 top-5 crushed-carton units are re-cartoned.
to10: Fix the held-stock math, remove the unnecessary stockout/backorder plan if rush lands on 7 Dec, and make the shade-level PO split tighter for the top 5 hero shades.

strength: It gives a practical cash-controlled order plan, rejects the bad ₹1.86 crore draft, protects hero matte shades, and has a good pro pre-book idea for makeup artists.
mistake: It gets the re-cartoning effect wrong: after re-cartoning, top-5 cover should rise, not stay at 2.4 weeks, so the December gap is overstated. It also delays some POs to 20 Nov without a strong reason.
to10: Place all POs on Monday, correct the top-5 cover to include re-cartoned stock, land the standard order earlier, and turn the backorder section into a contingency instead of the base plan.

strength: It clearly exposes the real issue: brand is hiding weak non-brand spend, and it ties the plan back to profit, feed health, bags, washable searches, and standing-all-day searches.
mistake: The $104,000 reserve and regional test make the plan feel less directly usable for a 30-day budget plan; some budget pacing details are also confusing, especially bags per-day spend and the expected profit math.
to10: Make the $240,000 spend plan cleaner and easier to approve, reduce the experimental complexity, and show a tighter expected-results calculation tied directly to each budget line.

strength: It gives me the exact owner-level answer I wanted: break-even ROAS, PMax without brand, what to cut, where to move spend, the feed fix first, title examples, and first-week actions in order.
mistake: The expected brand search value and PMax recovery assumptions are a little optimistic, so I would want the forecast softened or framed more clearly as a range.
to10: Add a slightly more conservative forecast and a clearer rule for how much of the reserve gets released if PMax does not improve after brand exclusions and feed fixes.

strength: It goes straight at the real leaks: delivery silence, bra fit, and a refund-first returns portal, with clear copy and sensible numbers.
mistake: The sales-kept figure from swaps is a ceiling and could be read as hard savings; I would label that more carefully and separate it from cost savings.
to10: Tighten the copy a little more in our playful voice, add a stronger customer-safe refund presentation in the portal mock-up, and show the test readout plan by metric and owner.

strength: The opening decision and target table are very owner-friendly, and the assumptions behind the projections are honest.
mistake: It invents specific November and December dates and the day-3 message logic is weaker for customers with no courier scan, which is the core WISMO problem.
to10: Remove the made-up calendar dates, make the no-scan customer update proactive, add a post-delivery bra fit follow-up, and make refunds feel equally clear rather than a smaller link.

strength: It gives the product team a buildable one-screen flow with exact copy, matched offers, and mostly sound revenue maths.
mistake: It keeps the 50% discount for switchers without evidence, and that weakens the principle of not using discounts unless the data supports them.
to10: Remove or test the switching-app discount instead of assuming it works, make the priority on rebuilding pause even sharper, and tighten the revenue assumptions for discounted users.

strength: It puts the pause first, avoids wasteful discounts, protects the cancel experience, and explains the business impact in a way I would act on next sprint.
mistake: The first-year revenue and discount-savings maths could be shown a little more plainly, and the trip-over path could offer a simple reminder for the next trip.
to10: Add the trip reminder option, show the 12-month revenue working more transparently, and include the exact price example for the annual switch in the copy.

strength: It goes straight at the three biggest avoidable causes, writes usable articles in our voice, and shows clear ticket-saving math.
mistake: The recommendation to merge or rework the payment article is not well supported; that article is already relatively helpful and probably needs better links more than a rewrite.
to10: Make the ticket forecast a clearer range, verify every product label, and remove the weaker merge recommendation for the payment article.

strength: The prioritisation is very sharp: it ranks by tickets we can remove, calls out the Apple/Google refund trap, and gives an honest savings range.
mistake: The articles are a bit less complete and ready to publish, especially the deleted-expense and Pro refund pages, and the first article states Simplify debts as certain when it should say 'probably'.
to10: Add fuller ready-to-publish steps for web, cancellation, and edge cases; soften the Simplify debts claim; and keep the article copy a little warmer and more complete.

strength: It gives the right straight answer on the 20% cut, shows the lifetime value math clearly, and focuses the programme around the top creator-educator partners instead of chasing more inactive affiliates.
mistake: The 40% first-year Partner tier is plausible, but the cost model is a little rough and could overpay top partners without a tighter cap or review rule.
to10: Tighten the Partner tier eligibility and budget controls, model the 90-day credit-window cost more carefully, and make the day-90 review criteria a bit more operational.

strength: The plan understands the real problem: this is a partner-retention and attribution issue, not a commission-rate issue. The 'Who sent you?' attribution test is a strong extra idea.
mistake: Some of the cost math is shaky, especially the projected cost of the 90-day window and the year-one savings from cutting only new referrals. I would not want to take those numbers to finance without reworking them.
to10: Fix the financial model, narrow the Partner tier so one manager can run it well, and fold the survey-attribution idea into the main plan instead of making it feel like an add-on.

strength: Nails the core insight — top-5 matte shades sell out during the season, rush + re-carton + honest back-order message — and delivers a dated, in-budget plan with an owner-voice customer line.
mistake: The 6-day gap is stated vaguely ('out from about 1 to 8 December') and the back-order/waitlist mechanic isn't fully tied to the numbers; the 3,200-unit demand waiting is mentioned but not built into a single ship-date commitment.
to10: Tighter gap accounting: exact units on back-order, the ship-by date, and the sale-moment cover confirmed with one running stock table the ops lead can update weekly.

strength: Sharpest arithmetic and decision structure: 76% to hero shades, exact rush/standard unit counts, back-order trigger at 300 units, and a concrete palette liquidation ladder with sell-through targets.
mistake: The customer-facing voice is thinner — the back-order line is clunky ('That's a real date') and there's no clean restock message for Tanvi; the pro pre-book idea is flagged as risky but left half-decided.
to10: A polished, on-brand honest restock line for Tanvi and a firmer call on the pro pre-book (yes/no with cap), plus one consolidated dated action list on top of the check sheet.

strength: It takes the 4.0 ROAS apart properly, shows non-brand loses money at 2.26 against a 2.5 break-even, and the $240,000 split adds up exactly with a clear reserve rule.
mistake: It fiddles a little too much at once (regional test, several changes on day 1-3) and it could be a touch clearer for a non-specialist reader in the first few lines.
to10: Trim the regional test to a footnote, tighten the opening sentence for grade-7 reading, and state the actual profit number today and expected on one line up front.

strength: It speaks in Rothy's voice and gives a clean, readable first-week checklist with practical feed-fix steps and title examples that use customer words.
mistake: The budget split has a $128,000 PMax line projected at 2.6 ROAS against a 2.5 break-even, but the cautious case shows it at 2.2, which would lose money, and the expected results table adds up to more value than today on less spend without a watertight explanation.
to10: Rebuild the budget with the same discipline as Output 1: non-brand PMax cut harder, brand search sized to actual demand, and an expected profit range that reconciles to the $240,000 ceiling with no double counting.

strength: Ruthless prioritisation: three fixes ranked by money saved, with the working shown, honest ranges, and a Christmas warning. The messages are short, warm, and in our voice with one button each.
mistake: The 'Still on track' message could still be sent when the courier has scanned but the parcel is delayed, risking a false reassurance; better to base it on actual tracking status, not just a scan.
to10: Make the day-3 message conditional on the latest tracking event (e.g., 'in transit' vs 'delayed') and include the tracking status in the copy, so we never imply on-time when the courier is behind.

strength: Comprehensive: six messages including a post-delivery fit check and a size-switch within 2 hours, plus concrete portal steps and a weekly feedback loop. The copy is clear and body-positive.
