mistake: The 2-hour size-switch window in message 2 assumes orders can be changed before picking; if not, the line must be dropped, which weakens the message. Also, the 'swaps keep £183,800 in sales' overstates because a swap is often one item, not the full £58 order.
to10: Tighten the numbers: show the swap value as the margin on the swapped item, not the full AOV, and give a range for sales kept. Make the 2-hour switch a verified capability before writing it into copy.

strength: It puts the pause at the centre, names it as the critical path, and is honest that without it the flow keeps fewer people than today. The per-reason matching and the margin logic on 'trip over' show real owner-level thinking.
mistake: The reminder panel's take-up is borrowed from the discount offer (9% take, 39% stay), which is a weak stand-in; the projection leans on it. Voice is warm but a few lines ('Pick one. It helps us help you.') drift toward retention-script phrasing.
to10: Tighter copy in Lena's own words on the pause panel and a clearer, sourced assumption for the reminder take-up, plus a one-line sensitivity so the £98k first-year figure is not the only number the team anchors on.

strength: It segments 'not making progress' by reminder status and adds a smaller-goal option, which is a genuinely different idea. The 12-month plan price breakdown (£4.95 a month, £59.40 once) is concrete and useful.
mistake: It keeps a 50% discount for 'switching apps' — the one group with no proven save — and shows the discount's 3.5% net stay as a save, which the owner explicitly flagged as counting discounted subscribers wrongly. It also adds a second 'smaller goal' offer tier without evidence, and its subscriber total (2,239) double-counts discounted people at full value.
to10: Drop the discount-for-switchers, fix the revenue maths to net of discount, and be honest that the 'not progressing' reminder and 'smaller goal' offers are untested guesses rather than quoting 3.5% as if it were a save rate.

strength: The ranked table is built on tickets we can actually remove, with clear arithmetic and a realistic range that shows its working; the three articles answer in the first two lines in plain, friendly language.
mistake: Treats 'Deleting expenses' as the main restore fix without checking that the existing article's 64% helpful rating means it is already addressing the right need; a better plan would keep and retitle it, not write a competing article.
to10: State the assumed skill of the writer and how the two-week plan fits one person's hours; include a one-line risk that retitling the delete article may confuse search; name the expected drop in the first paragraph so the owner sees the bottom line immediately.

strength: Covers more ground, including both app and web restore steps, search-term fixes, and a currency article in the forecast; the voice is calm and the first article's opening is strong.
mistake: The ticket forecast gives single-point estimates (like 40%) with weak justification; it also merges 'Recording a payment' despite it being 71% helpful, which contradicts the brief's warning about rewriting everything at once.
to10: Replace the single-point forecast with an honest range and show the range low/high; drop the merge of 'Recording a payment' or justify it with ticket data; add a realistic count of in-app link changes with engineer hours.

strength: Straight, honest answer on the 20% cut backed by lifetime-value maths, plus a complete tiers/payouts/first-30-days plan the one partner manager can actually run, all in Podia's plain cheerful voice.
mistake: The 90-day window cost is hand-waved ('may be the biggest cost... every 10% rise adds $63,000... review at day 90'), so the owner is asked to approve a spend they can't see sized; it should be estimated like Output 2 does.
to10: Put a firm dollar range on the 90-day window cost (and net it against the churn advantage), and name the partner tier thresholds in revenue terms, not just '10+ customers'.

strength: Sharpest read of the data: names the real problem as under-crediting not overpaying, quantifies the 90-day window cost ($62k-$89k), flags the written-promise risk, and adds a genuinely new idea (credit by 'Who sent you?').
mistake: Voice and tidy-up slip: a dated first-30-days table aimed at a specific week, legal/tax asides, and 'the bad news: this plan costs more' frames the plan defensively and drifts from Podia's friendly read; the 'bolder move' adds a second bet the owner has to weigh.
to10: Keep the insight but land it in Podia's voice: one clean plan, sized costs in the main flow, the 'who sent you' idea folded into the core timeline, and drop the table that dates the plan to one week.

strength: Takes the 4.0 apart against the 2.5 break-even, shows non-brand loses about $20k, and rebuilds the $240k split with a disciplined reserve rule and week-one order that starts with the feed fix.
mistake: The $104k reserve is very large and the bolder regional test adds complexity to a 30-day plan; the expected $198k profit leans on money deliberately left unspent, which could read as under-delivery rather than discipline.
to10: Tighter expected-range arithmetic shown step by step (including how the $198k is built from committed lines plus reserve), a smaller reserve with a clear deployment ladder, and the regional test demoted to an appendix so the core plan stays simple.

strength: Cleanest read: brand is 11% of spend and half the value, non-brand PMax loses about $36.7k a month, and the feed fix plus title examples are practical and in the brand's voice.
mistake: The forecast is over-optimistic and internally shaky: brand search at $18k returning 25 ROAS ($455k) and PMax at 2.6 after a cut imply a $1.11m value and 4.6 ROAS, and the cautious case at 2.2 PMax still claims $170k profit—numbers an owner will challenge, especially when brand buyers may not convert fully after the switch.
to10: A credible base and cautious case with the arithmetic shown, PMax target ROAS set at or above 2.5, and no brand-value inflation—plus a clear rule for what happens if the new non-brand Search campaign does not hit 2.8.

strength: All three articles are genuinely publishable and cover more ground than asked — app and web steps for restoring a delete, plus the cancel-subscription trap in the refund article.
mistake: It spends day 3 of a one-writer fortnight merging 'Recording a payment', an article already at 71% helpful, instead of leaving it alone and linking to it; and the forecast is one number plus a stress case rather than an honest range.
to10: Drop the merge, turn the forecast into a per-topic range with the same working, and keep the refund article to one task (refund) with cancel as a short linked note rather than a second procedure.

strength: Sharp editorial judgement: it explicitly says leave the 71% article alone and that nothing needs merging, leads with the bad news that 2,000 refund tickets are Apple's and Google's to solve, and gives a real per-topic range that reconciles to 15%–24% and $11.1k–$17.5k.
mistake: The reasoning leans on a loose benchmark — using the 71% helpfulness of a different article ('Recording a payment') as the ceiling for the new balances page — and it doesn't add the 'undo delete' search synonyms that Output 1 remembers.
to10: Replace the borrowed 71% benchmark with an argument grounded in this page's own data, add the search-synonym fix alongside the new title, and add web steps to the restore article.

strength: Dissects the 4.0 into profit per segment against a 2.5 break-even, puts the price-mismatch feed fix first, and builds a budget that adds to exactly $240,000 with a reserve rule, a downside range, and a bold regional test to challenge the 1.2.
mistake: Complicated to run: a reserve rule, a regional state-split test, and several simultaneous changes make week one hard to execute and the 13% reported-revenue drop may scare the CFO if not framed first.
to10: Trim to the essential moves (feed fix, brand exclusion, reallocation), push the regional test to a later month, and state the revenue/profit trade-off even more plainly up front.

strength: Cleanest read: brand is 11% of spend and 50% of value, PMax ex-brand is 2.03 and loses ~$36,700; a tidy split to $240,000, feed fix with concrete causes, and a usable title and ad copy rewrite.
mistake: Forecast relies on an aggressive PMax jump to 2.6 and brand at 25 ROAS after the switch; the plan is competent but less ambitious, with no test to prove the broad spend isn't building future brand demand.
to10: Add a way to test whether the 1.2 broad spend drives later brand demand, and show profit ranges per line rather than a single base case.

strength: Ranks the three fixes by money with the working shown, writes every message with one button and honest date ranges, and flags the Christmas/holdout caveat.
mistake: The swaps figure ('up to £61,000 to £97,000 of sales a month') is loose and overstates durable value; also the ticket count uses a rough 762/week baseline without weeks laid out.
to10: Tighten the swap value to net revenue kept after the £7.50 handling and next-size stock risk, with a clear low/high, and give a one-line expected total saving for the 60 days in a single figure range.

strength: Clean cost-of-inaction framing, six genuinely different messages with fit-check copy in our voice ('comfort beats the number on the tag'), and a tidy staged order of work.
mistake: The '£183,800 in sales kept' headline is a ceiling that oversells, and the fit-block language ('no gaps, no spilling over') drifts close to the shape-shaming tone we ban.
to10: Replace the sales-kept figure with realistic kept revenue net of handling, and soften the delivered fit guidance so it describes comfort and fit rather than how the body should look.

strength: Brings back the proven pause as the main save and makes it the critical path, with honest maths and a clear build order.
mistake: The pause acceptance rate and 90-day retention are assumed to repeat exactly; a test cell is mentioned but not sized.
to10: Add a small controlled test for the untested offers (annual switch, reminder) and a cash-flow view of the discount ending.

strength: Rich screen-level copy and extra segmentation (reminder status, daily goal) that feels warm and precise.
mistake: Keeps a 50% discount for 'switching apps', which the brief’s logic says to avoid, and applies it to a group where price match is dubious.
to10: Drop the broad discount, adopt the owner’s priority that the pause is 80% of the win, and tighten the arithmetic to show kept-at-full-price properly.

strength: Ranked by tickets we can actually remove, with honest math (2,961, 2,000, 4,900) and a low-end floor scenario an owner can bank on.
mistake: Three articles presented as 'ready to publish' still contain unverified UI steps (gear icon, Restore, Undelete expense) that a real writer would have to click through; also misses that 'Recording a payment' at 3,600 tickets deserves a link, not just a merge later.
to10: Verified step labels per platform, a single expected number plus range with the in-app link dependency called out explicitly, and flagging the settle-up link as a cheap high-ticket add.

strength: Executes the brief exactly as written: gap article planned properly, forecast given as a range of shares with a stated best-article benchmark (38% to 71%), and the Settle up link (3,600 tickets) captured, plus a bolder-move option with its risk.
mistake: Splits the Pro refund page out but doesn't say what happens to the existing 'Splitwise Pro billing' page (merged, kept, or its non-refund content moved) — a small ambiguity a writer would trip on.
to10: Say explicitly what the old Pro billing page becomes, add a per-article 'how we'll check it worked' line, and one sentence on which UI labels were verified vs assumed.

strength: Straight, well-argued no to the 20% cut with the lifetime-value maths and the break-even point, plus a clean, costed plan the one partner manager can actually run.
mistake: The 40% first-year Partner rate risks being read as a rate war and its 12-month maths is a small reach; a couple of cost lines (commissioned revenue impact) are estimates presented a bit tightly.
to10: Tighten the Partner 40%/new-customer cost model and state it as a test with a clear kill/scale rule, and add one line on what happens to the 4-of-20 retention risk if two leave.

strength: Sharpest insight in either piece — 'under-crediting, not overpaying' — plus the bold 'Who sent you?' credit idea and a dated, owner-assigned 30-day table.
mistake: The window-cost projection (1,250 new customers, 65-75% band) is a pile of assumptions stacked up, and one commission-cost range leans on a gross-margin figure it admits it doesn't have.
to10: Replace the projection with a small, bounded test (top 20, one quarter) and a stated cap on added commission, so the owner sees the downside before saying yes.

strength: Takes the 4.0 apart into profit per line against a 2.5 break-even, then hands over paste-ready titles, feed fields and ad copy in the same document, with a day-by-day first week.
mistake: It only adds a brand exclusion to Performance Max. Nothing actually switches off the $64,000 of broad 'women's flats' at 1.2 or the 'sustainable shoes' spend, and most of the claimed +$61,000 gain rests on brand search earning about 25x (a 40% jump on today's combined 18x) with no cautious case for it.
to10: Add negatives or a listing-group split that genuinely stops the broad and sustainable terms, show the numbers if brand only holds its current 18x instead of 25x, and warn me that Google-reported revenue will dip before profit rises.

strength: Shows that everything outside brand earned 2.26 and lost $20,100, quantifies the feed hole at $61,900 a month, and is honest that cutting the loss-makers drops reported revenue about 13% while profit rises; week 1 has an owner and a done-when on every step.
mistake: It commits only about $136,000 of the $240,000 and parks the rest, so the month deliberately shrinks rather than growing, and it gives no ready-to-paste ad copy and no expected value for brand search after the shift, which makes the profit bridge harder to check.
to10: Commit more of the ceiling to the proven lines with a stated expected brand-search value, add the paste-ready search ads and feed field fixes, and drop the odd unexplained '$59,948 a day' line.

strength: Strong, publish-ready articles in the right words, especially the undo-delete piece covering app and web.
mistake: It misses the cheap Settle up Help link for 3,600 recording-payment tickets and instead suggests merging a 71%-helpful article; the forecast is more point estimate than range.
to10: Add the Settle up screen link, drop or better justify the Recording a payment merge, and turn the ticket forecast into a clear range with explicit assumptions.

strength: The most owner-ready plan: right page priorities, smart use of the engineer day including the Settle up link, and a transparent ticket range with reasoning and risk.
mistake: The undo-delete article lacks web steps, and the Google Play refund path may need checking; the Settle up link is noted as upside but left out of the ticket range.
to10: Add web restore steps, verify the Apple/Google refund flows, include cancellation steps in the refund article, and either include the Settle up link in the range or show it as a separate conservative upside.

strength: It answers the three things in my data at once and makes them doable: no to the 20% cut with the lifetime maths, an invited top-40 Partner tier funded from the $40,000, and a dated, named 30-day plan (call the top 20 by 25 Nov, switch tracking, pay a month early). The one-page rules are written to be published, including plain-word disclosure, rel="sponsored", and a clause that earned commission stays earned.
mistake: Two of the numbers that carry the argument are asserted rather than shown. The 'about $38,000' saving from cutting only new referrals, and the '$62,000 to $89,000' credit-window cost, do not reconcile with the rates in the same document (the implied capture is 55-78%, not the stated 65-75%), so my finance lead will go straight at the two figures the plan rests on.
to10: Show the working on the $38,000 and the window cost in two short lines each, and put the 40%-for-12-months rival option on the table with its cost so I can see the cheaper tier was chosen on purpose, not by default.

strength: The cleanest reasoning of the two on the central question: 'we keep 70 cents, then 80 cents, so the cut breaks even at a 12.5% revenue drop' is checkable in one reading, and the churn-adjusted $158 / $106 / $211 per referred customer makes the competitive risk concrete. The 40%-first-12-months Partner tier is a real answer to the rival, costed at about $46,000.
mistake: It leaves the $50 minimum where it is, when minimum plus speed was 64% of survey comments, and the first 30 days are written as Days 1-7, 8-14 with no calendar dates or named owners, so my partner manager has to convert the plan before she can start it. The rules page also drops the '30 days' notice, earned commission stays yours' line that matters most if we ever touch terms.
to10: Put real dates and owners on the first 30 days, cut the Partner minimum to $25 and the standard to $50, add the notice and earned-commission clause to the rules, and state the credit-window cost as a range rather than 'may be the biggest cost.'

strength: Nails the core signal — top-5 matte shades out ~1 Dec, fix the crushed cartons Monday, rush the heroes, ignore the draft — and adds a pro pre-book and a clean clearance path for the palette, all inside ₹1.2 crore.
mistake: Minor arithmetic discipline slips: it says top-5 stock is 2.4 weeks even after re-cartoning (should become ~3.4 weeks), and the rush arrival date (7 Dec) is treated as tight against a 1 Dec stockout with back-orders used to bridge — workable but the timing story is slightly muddled.
to10: State the post-re-carton cover clearly (13,000 units, ~3.4 weeks, lasts to ~8 Dec), align the rush arrival to that date without needing back-orders, and confirm the party-pair economics (₹1,299 vs ₹1,998) are margin-positive.

strength: Crisp, owner-ready plan with a dated Monday action table, honest sold-out messaging in our voice ('back on 9 December, tap Notify me'), pro pre-orders for Farah, and a no-fake-urgency clearance for palettes — all inside ₹1.2 crore.
mistake: Sets the palette at ₹699 from 1 Dec and then bundles with kohl at ₹899, but doesn't check margin at the ₹310 floor or explain why ₹699 rather than full price first; also the 'out 30 Nov' then 'back 9 Dec' gap is longer than the re-cartoning buffer implies.
to10: Show the post-re-carton top-5 cover explicitly (13,000 units, ~3.4 weeks), tighten the stockout window to match, and prove the palette markdown and bundle still clear cost with a line of margin maths.

strength: Takes the 4.0 ROAS apart against the 2.5 break-even, puts the feed fix first, and gives a budget split that adds to exactly $240,000 with a base and cautious profit range.
mistake: The brand search forecast jumps to about 25 ROAS (from 17) and $455,000 value on $18,000, which looks optimistic and may overstate expected profit; the title strings are long and some wording (e.g. 'Women's Machine Washable Pointed Toe Flat') drifts from the brand's plain, warm voice.
to10: A more defensible brand forecast (conservative and base shown separately), tighter voice-checked title patterns, and a one-line explanation of how the reserve rule protects profit if lines underperform.

strength: Frames the whole month as brand hides losses in non-brand (2.26 ROAS), gives an honest warning that reported revenue will fall about 13%, and adds a genuine regional holdout test to check whether the cut spend was building brand.
